On the Art of Being Between

There is a moment, just before waking, when you are neither here nor there. You are not quite dreaming, but you are not yet awake. Your body is warm and heavy under the blankets, your breathing is slow, and the world has not yet demanded anything of you. No name, no obligations, no history. For a few seconds, you are simply a consciousness, floating. And then, like a tide returning, memory floods in. You remember who you are, where you are, what day it is, what you have to do. The self reassembles itself, piece by piece, until you are solid again.

I have always been fascinated by that in-between state. Not because it is mystical, although it feels that way, but because it reveals something true: that our solid, continuous selves are, in fact, constructions. We rebuild ourselves every morning. And if we can be unmade so easily by sleep, what else might we be able to unmake and remake while awake?

We live most of our lives in the middle. Between birth and death, between childhood and old age, between starting and finishing. We are taught to value the endpoints - the achievements, the arrivals, the conclusions - but almost all of living happens in the transit. The waiting rooms, the long drives, the years where nothing dramatic seems to be happening but everything is quietly shifting underneath. We call this ordinary life, as if it were the filler between the important parts, when in truth it is the important part itself.

Consider dust.

Everyone hates dust. It collects on shelves, under beds, on the tops of books that have been left unread for too long. We wipe it away without thinking. But dust is extraordinary. Every particle of dust in your room was once something else. Some of it is skin, yes, but some of it is soil from a field three miles away, carried in on the wind. Some of it is volcanic ash from an eruption that happened before you were born, still circling the globe in the high atmosphere. Some of it is stardust, literal fragments of meteorites that burned up on entry and drifted down for years before settling on your windowsill. The physicist's cliché is true: we are star stuff. But so is the dust on your bookshelf. So is the lint in your pocket. The universe does not distinguish between the majestic and the mundane. To the universe, a galaxy and a dust mote are made of the same ledger.

When you wipe away dust, you are, in a small way, participating in the great circulation of matter. You are moving the cosmos from one place to another. That is not a small thing.

We are taught to look for meaning on a large scale. We want our lives to be epic, cinematic. We want love to feel like a storm, work to feel like a calling, grief to feel profound and ennobling. And sometimes it does. But more often, life is quieter and stranger than that. It is making coffee at 7:14 on a Tuesday. It is noticing how the light falls through the kitchen window in October and realizing it falls at a slightly different angle than it did in September. It is hearing a song in a grocery store that you haven't heard in fifteen years and being suddenly, violently transported to a gymnasium in 2009. It is the way your friend laughs when they are truly surprised. These are tiny, almost invisible seams in the fabric of a day, and yet if you were to pull them together, they would be your entire life.

For a long time, I thought that to be a thoughtful person you had to be serious. You had to read difficult books and have strong opinions and speak in a low, considered voice. I have since learned that thoughtfulness is quieter than seriousness. It is not about having answers. It is about paying attention.

Attention is the rarest form of generosity. Simone Weil wrote that, and I believe it every time someone truly listens to me. Attention is also how we fall in love with the world again. Not by traveling to some distant, exotic place, but by looking, really looking, at the place we are already in.

Try this: tomorrow morning, look at something you have seen a thousand times - a chipped mug, a crack in the sidewalk, the tree outside your window - as if you have never seen it before. Pretend you are a traveler from another planet who has just landed and has no name for any of this. Notice the color, the texture, the way light interacts with it. Notice that the crack in the sidewalk is not just a crack; it is a tiny canyon filled with shadows, with a single resilient weed growing at its edge, with ants using it as a highway. Notice that your chipped mug holds the memory of every morning you have held it, the faint stain of a thousand coffees. If you do this for even thirty seconds, the object will stop being background and will become foreground. It will become alive.

This is not a trick. This is how children see the world before we teach them to categorize and dismiss. A child will spend twenty minutes watching a beetle cross a leaf. An adult will step over it without seeing it. We do not lose wonder because we grow old; we grow old because we lose wonder.

And wonder is not naive. Wonder is not ignorance. Quite the opposite - the more you know, the more wonderful things become. A botanist does not see less beauty in a flower because she knows its Latin name and its pollination strategy; she sees more. She sees the evolutionary history braided into its petals, the co-evolution with the bee that drinks from it, the physics of its color. Knowledge does not reduce magic; it deepens it. The universe is not less beautiful for being explicable. A rainbow is not less stunning because we understand refraction.

I think we are afraid of being in between because we are afraid of not knowing. We want to be certain. We want to know if we are on the right path, if we are good people, if our lives will matter. But certainty is a kind of death. A finished book cannot be written in anymore. A closed system cannot grow. The beauty of being human is that we are unfinished. We are drafts, constantly being revised. The philosopher Keats called this "Negative Capability" - the ability to be in uncertainties, mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact and reason. To be able to sit in the fog and not immediately need to disperse it.

The fog is where things grow.

Consider the mycelial network under a forest. If you walk through an old forest, you see individual trees, separate trunks, separate crowns. It looks like a collection of individuals competing for light. But underground, they are connected by a vast, white, branching net of fungus - the so-called Wood Wide Web. Trees share nutrients through it. Old trees nurse young trees. When one tree is attacked by insects, it sends chemical warnings through the mycelium to its neighbors. The forest is not a collection of individuals; it is a single, breathing superorganism. What looks like separation above ground is revealed as deep interconnection below.

We are like that too. We walk around feeling separate, sealed inside our skulls, convinced of our isolation. But we are constantly exchanging invisible signals - micro-expressions, tones of voice, pheromones, the shared air we breathe in a room. Our moods are contagious. Our ideas are not our own; they are composted from everything we have read, heard, and loved. Even our bodies are not entirely our own: half the cells inside you are bacterial, not human, living their own lives, helping you digest your food, influencing your mood. You are an ecosystem, not a monolith.

To remember this interconnection is not to lose yourself. It is to find yourself in a larger context. You are not a single note being played in isolation; you are part of a chord.

There is a story I return to often. It is about the Voyager probes. In 1977, we launched two small spacecraft, Voyager 1 and Voyager 2, into the darkness. They were meant to photograph the outer planets and then drift forever. We bolted a golden record to each of them, containing sounds and images from Earth - whale songs, a baby crying, Bach, Chuck Berry, greetings in fifty-five languages, the sound of a pulsar. Instructions for how to play it, in case anyone ever found it. It was a beautiful, hopeful, almost absurdly tender gesture: we put a mixtape on a bottle and threw it into the cosmic ocean.

Voyager 1 is now more than 15 billion miles away. It has crossed the heliopause, where the solar wind ends and interstellar space begins. It is the most distant human-made object in existence. Its power is fading; its instruments are shutting down one by one to conserve energy. Sometime around 2030, its transmitters will fall silent. It will continue to drift, forever, through the galaxy, at 38,000 miles per hour. In 40,000 years, it will pass within 1.6 light-years of a star called Gliese 445. It will not stop. It will not return.

And that record will still be there, silent and gleaming, long after the Earth itself is gone, long after the sun has become a red giant and swallowed our oceans. It will be a memory of a small, blue planet that once sang.

I tell this story not to make you feel small, but to make you feel immense. Because we did that. We, a species that still argues about trivial things and forgets to call our mothers, also did that. We looked into the abyss and decided to send music.

There is a temptation to think of time as an enemy. It takes from us. It wrinkles skin, erases memories, carries away people we love. But time is also the medium in which love becomes possible. Without time, there could be no growth, no healing, no learning. A peach needs time to ripen. A wound needs time to close. Time is not just loss; it is accumulation. Every day, you gather more layers - not just years, but textures. The scar on your knee from when you were seven. The word you learned last week that you now cannot imagine not knowing. The way you now know how to comfort a crying friend because you once were the one crying.

You are not losing time. You are becoming time.

And so we return to the in-between. Perhaps the most honest way to live is not to rush toward the next milestone, but to learn to dwell, with grace, in the transit. To love the unfinished sentence. To appreciate the house while it is still being built. To understand that you will never be "ready" or "done" or "perfectly healed," and that this is not a failure, but the very condition of being alive.

If you are in a waiting period right now - waiting for an answer, waiting for grief to soften, waiting to feel like yourself again - know that you are not wasting time. The waiting *is* the time. The chrysalis does not look like much from the outside. It hangs there, still and sealed. But inside, the caterpillar is liquefying itself, imagining wings it has never had.

There is a quiet work happening in you, even on days when you feel stagnant. The dust is settling. The mycelium is spreading. The light is shifting, degree by degree.

One day, you will wake up in that half-second between dreaming and remembering, and for a moment you will not know who you are. And instead of panicking, reaching immediately for the familiar scaffolding of your name and your tasks, you might linger there for just a breath longer. You might notice how spacious it feels to be nobody in particular, for just a moment. How open. How possible.

And then you will remember. You will get up, make your coffee, wipe the dust from the shelf, and carry on - not because you have arrived, but because you are still, beautifully, on your way.

Everything we love will become dust, and dust will become everything again. That is not a tragedy. That is a promise.
